headline: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says changing copyright law is about taking control of AI labs that already train on Australian creators' work without payment or consent.
score_reason: Pool score kept: the prime minister's strongest statement yet on AI and copyright in a country debating the issue, but only the opening of the report is available and the inquiry's advice is not law.
importance_line: Australian writers, musicians and other creators, and AI developers weighing whether to train models in Australia, are affected by a possible change to copyright rules, but the inquiry's advice is not law, its final report is due in November, and, as ABC News reports, independent senator David Pocock has alleged a stitch-up after the prime minister's office reviewed the committee's draft advice, which Labor and Coalition members deny.
summary: The Australian Financial Review reports that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday 13 Oct 2026, in his strongest comments yet in support of changing copyright law, that global AI labs are already using Australian creators' works to train their models without payment or consent and that the changes are about taking control of the situation, after a bipartisan parliamentary AI inquiry gave the green light to changes that would make it easier to train models in local data centres.
notes: AFR article is behind a subscription; only its opening paragraph was available. The committee's advice and the stitch-up row were read in ABC News (https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-13/ai-inquiry-independent-safety-watchdogs/107258612). Chosen LAW (copyright); could also sit in POL.
